content: NJIT needs a secure distance-learning environment that helps professors communicate and work with students online. Virtual-EDU should provide a classroom-like portal where enrolled users can communicate individually or in groups, share and collaborate on learning materials, and participate in online course activities. Administrators will also need to manage the learning environment and its enrolled users.

The main goal is to make remote learning feel organized, secure, and close to a real classroom experience. We want professors and students to be able to communicate easily, share course materials, work together on assignments, and take part in class activities without a lot of friction. It should feel natural for an enrolled student to join a course, follow along, interact, and get support from the instructor and classmates online.

The biggest issues are usually scattered communication, trouble finding the right materials, and too many separate tools that don’t work together well. Instructors also struggle with managing participation and keeping everyone engaged, while students can feel disconnected or unsure where to go for updates, assignments, or help. Security and access control are also important, because we need to make sure only enrolled users are in the course environment.

Migration would need to bring over the core course content and the active course structure so classes can keep running without restarting from scratch. In practice, that means materials like documents, slides, assignments, announcements, and maybe discussion history or shared resources, if those exist, along with enrolled users and their course memberships. We’d also want the usual workflows to carry over, such as submitting assignments, posting updates, and accessing the same course spaces, so instructors and students don’t lose momentum.

Yes, we’d want duplicates cleaned up and incomplete records flagged before anything is loaded, especially for user accounts and course enrollments. Legacy formats would need to be mapped into the new structure in a consistent way, and anything ambiguous should be reviewed instead of guessed at, because access and course membership have to be accurate. If some records can’t be converted cleanly, I’d expect them to be reported so the team can decide whether to correct them manually or leave them out.

For the first release, I’d want the basics fully working: secure login, course enrollment and access control, course pages, file sharing, communication between instructors and students, and the ability to post and submit course activities. Those are the pieces that make the environment useful on day one. Things like advanced analytics, extra integrations, and more polished collaboration features could probably come later if needed.

Yes, security and user access need to come first, because nothing else should be available until we know the right people are getting into the right courses. After that, the course structure and enrollment setup have to be in place before file sharing and class activities can really work properly. Communication can come alongside that, but it still depends on having the user and course context established first.

We’d consider the first release acceptable if instructors can run a class and students can join, communicate, access materials, and complete activities without major issues. It should be stable, secure, and usable enough that people don’t need workarounds for the basic teaching flow. For edge cases like failed enrollment or access problems, I know we’ll need a clear policy, but I’d want to confirm with the team whether those should be handled automatically, queued for review, or sent to an administrator for correction.

Yes, security has to win in any situation where there’s a risk of unauthorized access, especially around course membership, grades, or private communication. We’d rather make a legitimate user take one extra step than let the wrong person into a class or shared material. At the same time, for routine class tasks, we’d want the system to stay as simple as possible so students and instructors can actually use it without friction.

A typical class would start with students and instructors logging in, going to their course space, and seeing the materials, announcements, and activities for that course. Instructors would post content, share files, communicate with the class or with individual students, and set up assignments or participation activities, while students would review materials, ask questions, submit work, and join group discussions. Access might need to work differently for guest speakers, late add/drop changes, or special permission cases, but I’d want those handled in a controlled way so the normal class flow stays secure.

We definitely need it to support more than just a normal lecture course. Lab sections, discussion-based classes, and project or team-based courses are all likely, and some instructors may want to run hybrid classes where part of the work is online and part is in person. I’m not sure yet whether there are special cases like cross-listed courses or guest instructor access, but those are the kinds of scenarios we should verify.

I don’t have exact numbers yet, so I’d need to confirm that with NJIT enrollment data and whoever owns the academic systems. My expectation is that normal daily use will be much lower than peak usage, but registration periods, exam weeks, and the start of term will drive noticeable spikes. We should plan for those busy windows so the system stays responsive even when many students are logging in at the same time.

Yes, I would expect at least some of those cases, especially cross-listed courses and guest instructors. Cross-listed classes would need to behave like one shared course space even if students are coming from different departments, and guest instructors would likely need limited access rather than full control. I’d want to confirm the exact rules for those exceptions before locking down the design.

The main distinction is between the official course section and the smaller groups inside it, because instructors may want to address the whole class or just a lab or project team. Learning activities should also be clearly separate from content, since something like an assignment, quiz, or discussion has different handling than a file or announcement. I’d also want the terminology to match what NJIT faculty and students already use, so it feels familiar instead of forcing new labels.

I’d keep the official term as the course section, since that’s the enrolled class tied to NJIT records. For smaller cohorts, labels like lab group, project team, or discussion group would make sense depending on the teaching context, and the system should let the instructor name them in a way that fits the course. In some cases the same group might be referred to both by its functional name and by its section affiliation, especially when multiple sections share a resource or activity space.

For the first release, I’d expect those problems to be queued for review rather than corrected automatically. If a student can’t get into the right section or group, the system should flag it clearly and route it to an administrator or support staff member who can verify the record and fix it safely. Automatic correction sounds risky at this stage unless the rule is very simple and we’re completely confident in the source data.

Administrators should be able to create, deactivate, and update user accounts, and assign people to the right roles like student, instructor, TA, or guest. They’ll also need to create or manage course shells, control who can access a course or group, and adjust permissions when instructors need extra help or when access has to be restricted. I’d also expect some ability to monitor activity and intervene if there’s a policy or security issue.

Virtual-EDU should support sections that have different meeting patterns, because labs and discussions often run on a separate schedule from the main lecture. It should also allow split access where one group can see only the materials or activities meant for them, especially in project-based or hybrid setups. In practice, the activity structure may vary by format, so the system needs enough flexibility for instructors to organize content, assignments, and group work differently from one course to the next.

For the shared course space, I’d lean toward a single common set of rules so students aren’t getting conflicting access in the same environment. If a department needs a different restriction, that should probably be handled through role-based exceptions or separate subgroups, not by making the whole shared space behave differently. I’d want the system to support exceptions, but only in a controlled way so the overall course stays consistent.

Role-based exceptions are the most important, like letting instructors and TAs see more tools or manage submissions while students have limited access. Subgroup exceptions should also be allowed for things like lab sections, project teams, or accommodated students who need different materials or due dates. I would not want ad hoc exceptions that let a single user bypass the course’s main visibility rules unless there is a formal admin-approved reason, because that gets hard to audit and could create fairness issues.

The main rule should be the teaching purpose: if the subgroup is tied to instruction delivery, like a lab or discussion, it should follow the course structure; if it’s for collaboration, then project teams make sense; and if it’s for accessibility or special support, then accommodation-based groups should be allowed. The instructor or admin should choose the subgroup type, but the system should require a clear reason so it’s not just an arbitrary grouping. I’d also expect the subgroup to inherit some permissions from the parent course, unless there’s a specific approved exception.

Yes, if it’s relevant to the whole course it should surface in the main course space, even if it was posted from a subgroup or by a specific role. If it’s meant only for that subgroup, then it should stay hidden from everyone else, but there should still be a clear indication that something exists for the people who have access. The visibility rule should follow the content’s audience, so students only see what applies to them and staff can see the full context.

The system should keep the section schedule attached to each activity type, so a lecture, lab, or discussion shows its own meeting time and location or online room. If a student is enrolled in multiple related sections, it should clearly separate what applies to each one and avoid duplicating the same update everywhere unless it is meant to be shared. I’d also want the calendar and reminders to respect the student’s actual section assignments so they only get the activities that affect them.

The student should only see calendar entries and reminders for the sections they’re currently assigned to, and anything from an old section should drop off once the change is effective. If they’re in multiple sections, the system should show all applicable items, but it should make it obvious which section each one belongs to so they can tell them apart. When a section change happens, reminders tied to that section should update automatically instead of leaving stale notices behind.

Already sent reminders probably shouldn’t be erased from the user’s history, because that would be confusing and bad for auditing. But anything still upcoming should be updated in place if the change is known early enough, and if a reminder or calendar item no longer applies, it should disappear from the active view. During the transition, I’d want a short grace period only if needed for sync delays, but not long-term visibility of outdated items.

The main rule should be that course-wide items are separated from section-specific and subgroup-specific items, and each post or file needs a clear label showing who it applies to. Important participation-related notices, like deadlines, attendance expectations, or discussion requirements, should always be surfaced in the student’s main view if they affect them, with a link back to the detailed section or group context. I’d also want a single “priority” or “important” flag for urgent updates so students don’t miss something just because it was posted in a lower-traffic area.

For messaging, I’d expect it to feel near real time during normal use, so sending and receiving should happen within a few seconds at most. File uploads should show progress and be able to handle larger course materials without timing out too easily, though I don’t know the exact size limit yet and would need to confirm that. For activity participation, it should count as recorded as soon as the system confirms the submission or action was received successfully, not just when the student clicks submit.

Yes, slower loads are acceptable in those cases, especially for large files, rich media, or a first-time access when the system has to initialize everything. In normal day-to-day use, though, the course space should still feel responsive, and content should appear progressively if it can’t load all at once. If the network is weak, it’s more important that the user sees partial content and a clear loading state than a blank screen.

Anything posted in a section or group should stay visible only to the members of that section or group by default. It should become course-wide only if the poster intentionally shares it at that level, or if the instructor has set it as an announcement that everyone needs to see. Private messages between individuals should remain private unless there’s an explicit reason to forward or copy them.

Instructors should be able to post, edit, and remove course content in their own sections, and administrators should have override access if there’s a support or policy reason. Students should usually only be able to create and edit their own contributions, like discussion posts or uploaded assignments, and they shouldn’t be able to change or delete someone else’s material. If content is shared to a group space, then members of that group may need limited editing rights for collaborative work, but I’d want the instructor to control whether that is allowed.

Administrators should only view the user data they need for their job, and anything sensitive should be restricted by role and logged for audit purposes. If they need to intervene in an account or override access, that should be allowed for support, security, or policy enforcement, but not casually, and we should probably limit that to designated admins. I’d expect some actions, like changing roles or deactivating an account, to require approval or at least a second review in special cases, especially if it affects faculty accounts or an active student record.

For user accounts, I’d only merge automatically when the match is very strong, like the same institutional ID or a verified email plus matching name and status. If there’s any conflict in identity details, role, or enrollment history, it should go to manual review instead of guessing. Course enrollments should be excluded from auto-merge unless the course code, term, and user identity all line up cleanly, because a bad merge there could put someone in the wrong class or hide a real enrollment.

Course records should definitely be kept for a period of time after the course ends, because faculty and administration may need access for audits, grade disputes, or accreditation purposes. My assumption is that they would be archived rather than deleted in normal cases, and then only removed if there’s a formal retention policy or legal reason to do so. I don’t know the exact retention period yet, so that would need to be confirmed with NJIT policy.

Keep it in a limited form for manual correction and review. Excluding it entirely could make it harder to trace what went wrong, especially during migration or reconciliation, so it’s better to preserve the record with flags showing that it needs attention. That way admins can correct it without losing the original information.

They should stay accessible according to NJIT’s records retention and academic policy, and I’d expect archived access for a defined period rather than open access forever. Certain records, like those tied to grade disputes, audits, accreditation, or legal holds, should be kept longer and possibly restricted to authorized staff only. I don’t know the exact timeframes or any special exceptions offhand, so those would need to be confirmed with the university’s policy team.

Yes, but only in exceptional cases, like troubleshooting a support issue, resolving a grading dispute, or handling an urgent administrative matter. Before granting it, I’d want documented approval from an appropriate supervisor or system owner, a clear reason, a time limit, and confirmation of exactly which data or function the person can access. It should also be fully logged so we can see who approved it, who received it, what they accessed, and when it expired.

I’d expect the system to immediately contain the issue by disabling the affected account or access path, preserving logs, and preventing any further changes if possible. Support should escalate right away to security and the appropriate NJIT administrators, and any notification to users or leadership should follow the university’s incident response and privacy rules. If there’s data loss, we’d also want recovery from backup where appropriate, but only after the incident is controlled and the impact is understood.

Yes, I could see rare cases like accessibility support, compliance reviews, or a temporary research-related need if a course is being used for an approved academic purpose. I’d still want approval from the system owner or a designated dean-level administrator, with the access limited to the smallest necessary scope and a defined expiration time. The access should be logged the same way as any other exception, including the request, approver, timeframe, and what was actually accessed.

Notification should go to the people who need to respond first, like security, IT support, and the relevant NJIT administrator, and then to affected faculty or students only if the incident actually impacts them. We should keep the message minimal at first, sharing only what’s necessary to explain the issue and any required action, without exposing more student data than needed. If there’s any chance the incident involves privacy or legal implications, I’d want the communication reviewed before it goes out to the broader audience.

Yes, I’d want the log to include the reason for the exception and any conditions attached, like whether the access was read-only or limited to a single course or student record. It would also be useful to note who is allowed to review that log entry, since some of those details may need to be restricted to security or administrators only. That keeps the audit trail complete without making it broadly visible.

Security staff and authorized system administrators should definitely be able to review them, and I’d also expect audit or compliance personnel to have access when needed. If the entry includes sensitive exception details or student-specific information, then yes, visibility should be tighter by role, so faculty or general support staff would only see what they need for their job. In those cases, the most sensitive parts should be limited to the smallest set of approved reviewers.

I’d base that on least privilege, so each role should only see the details needed to do their job. For example, administrators might see the full audit record, while faculty or support staff could see only a summary or the parts relevant to their case, and student-specific data should be masked unless they are explicitly authorized. If there’s any doubt, the safer default would be to hide the sensitive fields until an approved reviewer needs them.

In most cases I’d expect those exceptions to be read-only, especially if the access is just for troubleshooting, review, or a temporary lookup. Editing or other actions should only be allowed when the exception was explicitly approved for that purpose, like a grading correction or an administrative update, and even then it should be tightly limited and logged. If it’s not clearly necessary, I’d keep it read-only by default.

The initial notice should cover the basic facts: that there is an incident, what part of the portal or course access is affected, who is impacted in general terms, and what immediate steps people should take. It should hold back any detailed student information, technical root-cause speculation, or anything that hasn’t gone through privacy or legal review yet. Later updates can fill in those details once the situation is confirmed and cleared for release.

They should get a short alert saying the communication feature is unavailable or limited, what action they need to take next, like using email or waiting for restoration, and whether any deadlines or class activities are being impacted right away. That first message should not include sensitive student data, internal investigation details, or anything that could be misleading before the issue is fully reviewed. If privacy or legal review is involved, I’d keep the notice very general until they clear it.

Yes, I’d expect some built-in guidance for first-time users, especially professors and administrators since they’ll be using more of the portal’s features. A short walkthrough or contextual tooltips would be helpful, and for students we’d want simple guidance on joining classes, submitting work, and messaging. I don’t think it needs to be a full training system inside the portal, but it should be easy enough for new users to get started without much help.

I’d want the portal to retry automatically for a short period and let the sender know that delivery is delayed. If it still can’t go through, it should queue the message so it can be sent once service is restored, rather than dropping it silently. The sender should also get a clear status so they know whether they need to try another channel.

Yes, there should be limits so messages do not sit there indefinitely. I’d expect retries for a short window, and if it still fails after that, the message should either stay queued for a defined period or be marked failed and the sender notified, depending on how critical the message is. The sender should get a different notice when it is still pending versus when it has expired or failed, so they know whether to wait or resend by another method.

I’d expect NJIT’s IT or LMS support team to own the day-to-day support after release, including user issues, routine fixes, and coordinating updates. The development team would probably handle larger bugs or planned enhancements during the warranty or transition period, but not be the main support contact forever. For professors and students, there should be a clear support path so they know who to contact when something goes wrong.

Routine account, access, password, class enrollment, and how-to questions should stay with NJIT IT or LMS support. Anything that looks like a product defect, data corruption, repeated outage, or a security issue should be escalated to the development team, and anything with privacy or legal implications should also involve the right campus office. If it’s unclear, I’d rather have support triage it first and then pass it along quickly than send users back and forth.

If the issue involves student records, personal data, accessibility, disciplinary concerns, or anything that could violate policy, NJIT IT or LMS support should stop short of making a judgment and escalate it. They can handle the technical side if it is clearly routine, but once there is any real privacy or compliance risk, the campus office that owns that policy area should take over. I’d have support make the initial triage call using a simple checklist, and if there is any doubt, escalate rather than guess.

Immediate handoff should happen if the case involves unauthorized access, exposure of personal or academic records, suspected cheating or misconduct, or any security incident. It should also be escalated right away if the user is asking for an exception to policy, or if the issue affects multiple users or a critical class function and looks bigger than normal troubleshooting. If it is just a login, navigation, or simple feature issue with no policy or security concern, support can keep working it.

If there is any clear evidence of data being viewed, changed, or shared by the wrong person, that should be enough for immediate handoff. Also, if the issue has been reproduced more than once, affects more than one account, or suggests a system-wide flaw, support should stop normal troubleshooting and escalate. In practice, I’d rather the threshold be low, because it is better to involve the right office early than to let a sensitive issue linger.
